Breadboard test

Wire the clock's electronics up on a breadboard and check every part works, before you solder anything or print the case. You add one part at a time and test it, so if something doesn't work you know exactly where to look. No soldering is needed except for the parts that only come with solder pads (the USB-C breakout, the LED and the ring). Allow an evening.

Before you start

How a breadboard works

Three kinds of jumper wire

With the ESP32 plugged in, a wire to one of its pins goes into a free hole in the same row of five as that pin, so those ends are male. Modules have pins, so their end of a wire is female.

The ESP32 sits next to the breadboard and you connect to its pins with the female end of a jumper. Most modules have pins too, so a female–female jumper goes straight from the ESP32 to the module.

Wire colours used here

3.3 V5 Vground (GND)signals

Your jumpers can be any colour, but sticking to red for 5 V, orange (or another one colour) for 3.3 V and black for ground makes mistakes easy to spot.

⚠️ Golden rules. Unplug the USB cable (and later the 5 V adapter) every time you change wires. Keep the ESP32 on your computer's USB the whole time and never connect the 5 V adapter to its 5V pin. Make sure the two ground rails stay joined.

You'll also want the two small 6 × 6 mm push buttons from your tactile switch kit; the 16 mm panel buttons need soldering, so they go in during final assembly.

1

Flash the firmware

⏱ 10 min

No wiring yet. Get the ESP32 running first, on its own, so you know the board and the firmware are good before anything else is connected.

You need: ESP32-S3 boardUSB-C data cableComputer
  1. Plug the USB-C cable into the port marked USB on the ESP32 (the board has two; this one carries the log).
  2. Flash the firmware from the Firmware page: the web flasher needs nothing installed.
  3. Open a serial monitor at 115200 baud (the web flasher has one, or PlatformIO's monitor).
  4. On your phone, join the Wi-Fi network CeilingClock-Setup and pick your home network.
✅ Test it: Open http://ceilingclock.local/ on your phone or computer. You should see the clock's page with the time and a green synced just now.
Not working?
ceilingclock.local doesn't open
Some Android phones don't support .local names. Use the IP address printed in the serial monitor instead.
Nothing in the serial monitor
Use the port marked USB, not UART, at 115200 baud. Some USB-C cables only carry power: try another.
No CeilingClock-Setup network
Press the RST button on the ESP32 and wait 20 seconds.
2

ESP32 onto the breadboards, and power rails

⏱ 10 min

The ESP32 is too wide for one breadboard: on one board its pins would cover every free hole. Two boards side by side give each row of pins its own board, with free holes beside every pin. Then three short wires set up the rails: the top rails become 3.3 V and ground, the bottom rails ground for the 5 V supply.

You need: 2 full-size breadboards (830 holes)3 jumper wires: 3 male–male
⚠️ Leave the row of the ESP32's 5V pin (row 25, lower board) empty.

New wires are bright and numbered; earlier ones are faded. Hover a wire in the list to find it in the picture.

  1. Unplug the USB cable.
  2. Put the two breadboards side by side, both the same way round, so column j of one board sits next to column a of the other, with two rail strips between them. Leave all the rail strips on.
  3. The pictures show the boards turned a quarter turn so row 1 is on the left. If yours stand upright with row 1 at the top, the left board is the lower board and the right board is the upper board.
  4. Turn the ESP32 so its antenna points toward row 1. Its row of pins starting with 3V3 goes into column j of the lower board; the row starting with GND, TX, RX goes into column a of the upper board. The first pins go in row 5. It sits over the two middle rail strips, which stay unused. Press down evenly on both rows of pins, not on the metal can.
  5. If the pins don't quite reach columns j and a on your boards, use i and b instead, or pull one middle rail strip off and push the boards together. What matters is that each pin has free holes beside it on the outside: the free holes in the same row of five as a pin are connected to that pin.

Connect

✅ Test it: Plug the USB cable back in: the clock starts as before. With a multimeter, the top + and − rails read about 3.3 V. Before you measure, check the meter's red lead is in the socket marked V, not A or mA, and the dial is on DC volts: on amps the meter shorts the supply and the ESP32 restarts.
Not reading 3.3 V on the rails? Check in this order
  1. Set the meter up. Red lead in the V socket, not A or mA: this is the most common mistake, and on amps the meter shorts the supply (the ESP32's light flashes as it restarts). Turn the dial to DC volts (V with a straight line; the 20 V range if it isn't auto-ranging). Black lead in COM. Meter probes are often too thick to reach the metal inside a breadboard hole: push the male end of a spare jumper into the hole and touch the probe to that instead.
  2. Is the ESP32 on? With the USB cable in the port marked USB, the board's small power LED should be lit and the clock's page should open. If not, try another cable and USB port before anything else.
  3. Measure on the ESP32 itself. Red probe on the solder joint of the 3V3 pin, black on the joint of a G pin. It should read about 3.3 V. If it reads 0 V, the board isn't getting power (cable or port). If it reads well under 3 V, or the board gets warm, unplug at once and look for solder bridging two header pins.
  4. Measure the 3V3 pin's row. Keep black on the G joint and put red in hole i5, lower board. 3.3 V here means the pin is making contact. 0 V means it isn't: press the ESP32 down firmly (the pins should disappear into the holes), and count the rows to check the 3V3 pin is really in the row you think.
  5. Measure the + rail. Keep black on the G joint and put red in the top + rail, near where the orange wire goes in. 0 V here: the orange wire isn't in the rail (check it is in the rail row by the red line, marked +, not the blue − row), or the jumper is broken: swap it for another.
  6. Check the rail runs the whole length. Many full-size breadboards split each rail in the middle; look for a break in the red and blue lines halfway along. Put red in the + rail at the far end. If it reads 0 V there but 3.3 V near the wire, the rail is split: bridge the two halves with a short jumper, on the − rails too.
  7. Measure + rail to − rail. Now red in the top + rail, black in the top − rail. If the earlier checks passed but this reads 0 V, the − rail isn't connected to ground: check the black wire from hole b5, upper board (the ESP32's first GND pin) to the top − rail.
  8. Reads −3.3 V. The probes are swapped. Nothing is wrong.
  9. The ESP32's light flashes when you touch the probes on. Stop: the meter is shorting the supply and the board restarts each time. Usually the dial is on current (A or mA) or the red lead is in the A or mA socket: move it to V and the dial to DC volts. On amps the meter can blow its internal fuse, so check it on a battery afterwards. Otherwise a probe tip is touching two pins at once, or the black probe is touching the RST pin (it sits next to the 3V3 pins): probe the breadboard holes rather than the pins.
  10. No meter? Skip ahead to the buttons and the front display: if they work, the rails are fine.
Not working?
The ESP32 doesn't start on the breadboard
A pin may be folded under the board. Lift it out gently, straighten the pin and press it in again.
The ESP32 goes dark when you add the wires
The orange wire is in a ground row or rail. It must start in the row of the first pin (3V3) and end in the top + rail.
3

Buttons

⏱ 10 min

For testing, use two small 4-legged push buttons; the 16 mm panel buttons go in later. Each one sits across the gap in the middle of the breadboard. Wire to diagonally opposite legs: that way it works whichever way round the button sits. On the lower board the rows beside the ESP32 are taken, so the buttons go at the two ends.

You need: 2 small 6 × 6 mm push buttons (from your tactile switch kit)4 jumper wires: 4 male–male

New wires are bright and numbered; earlier ones are faded. Hover a wire in the list to find it in the picture.

Place the parts

  1. Push button A across the gap in the middle: two legs in row 1, two in row 3, one each side of the gap (lower board).
  2. Push button B across the gap in the middle: two legs in row 28, two in row 30, one each side of the gap (lower board).

Connect

✅ Test it: On the clock's page, press button B: the Front display button on the page flips between on and off. Now press B and keep holding it: 3 seconds after you pressed, Projector flips on the page (the page can take another second to show it). Let go after it flips; letting go sooner counts as a short press. (Button A snoozes an alarm; you'll try it later.)
Not working?
Nothing happens
Check the wires go to diagonally opposite legs (j1 and a3, j28 and a30) and that the button straddles the gap.
It acts as if always pressed
The button is turned so both wires land on legs that are always connected. Turn it 90°.
4

Front display (TM1637)

⏱ 5 min

The four-digit display that shows the time on the front of the clock. Its two data pins go straight to the ESP32; power comes from the top rails.

You need: TM1637 display4 jumper wires: 4 female–male

New wires are bright and numbered; earlier ones are faded. Hover a wire in the list to find it in the picture.

Connect

✅ Test it: The display shows the time within a second. On the settings page, change the front display's brightness: it follows.
Not working?
Display stays blank
CLK and DIO swapped? VCC must go to the + rail (3.3 V).
Shows 88:88 or garbage
A loose jumper: push each one firmly onto its pin.
5

Projector LCD (Nokia 5110)

⏱ 10 min

The LCD makes the image on the ceiling. Test it as it comes, before cutting its window: lighting its own backlight lets you read it on the bench.

You need: Nokia 5110 LCD (no need to cut it yet)8 jumper wires: 8 female–male

New wires are bright and numbered; earlier ones are faded. Hover a wire in the list to find it in the picture.

Connect

✅ Test it: The LCD shows the time, back to front: the clock mirrors it for the projector. Untick Mirror left/right in the projector settings to read it, and tick it again before testing the optics.
Not working?
Blank or solid black
Adjust LCD contrast on the settings page. Check RST and CE.
No backlight
On some boards BL lights when connected to + instead of −. Move that one wire to the top + rail.
6

Light sensor

⏱ 5 min

This step uses two separate parts: the light sensor and a 10 kΩ resistor. The sensor alone does nothing: the resistor sits under it, between the sensor and ground, and the ESP32 reads the voltage where the two meet. That voltage rises as the room gets brighter. Neither part has a right way round. They go on the upper board, next to the 3.3 V rail.

You need: GL5528 light sensor (round disc)10 kΩ resistor (a separate part: striped cylinder)2 jumper wires: 2 male–male
⚠️ Two parts, not one. If you only put the round sensor in, the reading sits near 4095 whatever the light. And check the resistor is 10 kΩ (ten thousand ohms), not 10 Ω: they come in the same kind of bag, and 10 Ω reads near 0 all the time.

New wires are bright and numbered; earlier ones are faded. Hover a wire in the list to find it in the picture.

The two parts

Place the parts

  1. Light sensor (the round disc with a squiggly line on it): legs in h13 and h16 (upper board). Either way round.
  2. 10 kΩ resistor (bands brown-black-orange, or brown-black-black-red on 5-band resistors; the BOJACK bag says 10KΩ): one leg in j16, the same row as the sensor's second leg; the other leg in the top − rail (the row by the blue line), about row 17 (upper board). Either way round.

Connect

✅ Test it: In the night settings, watch sensor now next to "Dark below". It goes up with a torch on the sensor and down when you cover it with a finger.
Not working?
Always about 0
The sensor leg isn't in row 13 or the orange wire isn't on the + rail.
Always about 4000 or more, even in a dim room
The ESP32 is seeing the full 3.3 V. Either the 10 kΩ resistor is missing or isn't reaching the − rail (one leg in the same row as the sensor's second leg, row 16; the other in the − rail by the blue line), or the pink wire is in the sensor's first row (13, the 3.3 V side) instead of row 16.
7

Clock module (DS3231)

⏱ 5 min

The battery-backed clock that keeps time when Wi-Fi or power drops. Its two data pins are on the ESP32's top edge (pins 1 and 2), so these two wires start on the upper board.

You need: DS3231 module (with its coin cell)4 jumper wires: 4 female–male

New wires are bright and numbered; earlier ones are faded. Hover a wire in the list to find it in the picture.

Connect

✅ Test it: The page shows RTC backup ok. Turn your router's Wi-Fi off and press RST on the ESP32: the time is still right.
Not working?
Still says "no RTC"
SDA and SCL swapped, or VCC on 5 V instead of 3.3 V.
ZS-042 (larger) board
It charges its battery. With a non-rechargeable CR2032, remove the 200 Ω resistor or diode beside the holder first.
8

5 V supply

⏱ 10 min

From here on, parts need more current than the ESP32 can give. The 5 V supply feeds the bottom rails only. The ESP32 stays on your computer's USB, and the grounds are already joined.

You need: USB-C breakout + 5 V 3 A adapter2 wires soldered to VBUS and GND (or header pins)
⚠️ Never connect this 5 V to the ESP32's 5V pin while the computer is plugged in: two supplies would fight through the board. In the finished clock the computer stays unplugged.

New wires are bright and numbered; earlier ones are faded. Hover a wire in the list to find it in the picture.

Connect

✅ Test it: Plug the adapter in. Everything carries on as before. With a multimeter, the bottom rails read about 5 V.
Not working?
Reads 0 V
Some breakouts only switch on with a USB-C to USB-C charger and 5.1 kΩ CC resistors (yours has them). Try another cable.
9

Amplifier and speaker

⏱ 10 min

Plays the alarm sounds. The amplifier comes with its pins loose, so solder those first (below). The capacitor steadies its supply; the long leg is +, and the stripe marks −.

You need: MAX98357A amplifier with its 7-pin header and blue screw terminal (in its bag)40 mm speaker100 µF capacitorSoldering iron and solder5 jumper wires: 5 female–male

New wires are bright and numbered; earlier ones are faded. Hover a wire in the list to find it in the picture.

Solder the amplifier first

  1. Header first. Push the 7-pin strip into any free spot on the breadboard, long ends down. Lay the amplifier on the short ends, chip side up, and solder all 7. Start with one end pin, check the board sits flat, then the other end, then the rest.
  2. Then the screw terminal. Lift the board off the breadboard. Sit the blue block on the chip side at the other edge, wire openings facing outward. Turn the board over and solder its two pins from underneath.
  3. Check every joint with a bright light: shiny cones, and no solder joining two neighbouring pins (look hardest between GAIN and SD).
  4. Wire it up as below. Leave GAIN and SD unconnected.

Place the parts

  1. 100 µF capacitor: the long leg (+) in the bottom + rail at row 19, the leg by the stripe (−) in the bottom − rail at row 20. This one does have a right way round.

Connect

✅ Test it: Screw the speaker leads into the amp's + and − terminals. Under Sounds, press Play on beep.wav: four beeps. Then give an alarm a radio or podcast URL and press Preview stream.
Not working?
Silent
Is the 5 V adapter plugged in? Check BCLK, LRC and DIN aren't swapped. Leave GAIN and SD unconnected.
Crackles
Push the capacitor's legs fully into the rails (long leg to +).
10

Sunrise ring

⏱ 10 min

The sunrise light. The 330 Ω resistor protects the ring's data input; the big capacitor smooths the current the LEDs draw. Mind the capacitor's stripe: it goes to −.

You need: WS2812B 16-LED ring (with leads soldered on)330 Ω resistor (orange-orange-brown)1000 µF capacitor4 jumper wires: 3 female–male, 1 male–male

New wires are bright and numbered; earlier ones are faded. Hover a wire in the list to find it in the picture.

Place the parts

  1. 330 Ω resistor (bands orange-orange-brown, or orange-orange-black-black): legs in c15 and c19 (lower board). Either way round.
  2. 1000 µF capacitor: the long leg (+) in the bottom + rail at row 23, the leg by the stripe (−) in the bottom − rail at row 24. This one does have a right way round.

Connect

✅ Test it: Give an alarm a sunrise time (for example 15 minutes) and press Ring now: the ring glows warm white until you press Dismiss (or hold button A for 2 seconds).
Not working?
Nothing lights
Make sure the wire goes to DI (in), not DO (out). Check the 5 V adapter is on.
Flickers or wrong colours
Keep the data wire short. If it persists, a 74AHCT125 level shifter on the data line fixes it.
11

Projector LED

⏱ 15 min

The bright LED that lights the LCD. The MOSFET module switches and dims it for the ESP32. The 4.7 Ω resistor limits the current to about 400 mA, and it gets warm, so keep it off the plastic.

You need: MOSFET module3 W LED on its star (leads soldered on)4.7 Ω 2 W resistorSomething metal to sit the LED on2 jumper wires: 2 female–male
⚠️ Don't look straight into the lit LED. Without its heatsink it heats up in seconds: sit the star on metal and don't leave it at full brightness for more than a few seconds.

New wires are bright and numbered; earlier ones are faded. Hover a wire in the list to find it in the picture.

Place the parts

  1. 4.7 Ω 2 W resistor (the big one; bands yellow-violet-gold, or yellow-violet-black-silver): legs in c22 and c26 (lower board). Either way round.

Connect

✅ Test it: On the clock's page, switch the Projector off and on: the LED goes off and on. Change the projector's day brightness: it dims.
Not working?
LED never lights
LED + and − swapped? Check OUT+ goes through the resistor to LED +.
Always on full
TRIG is on the wrong pin, or the module's trigger GND isn't connected.

2

ESP32 onto the breadboard, and power rails

⏱ 10 min

The ESP32 plugs into the left end of the breadboard, with its antenna sticking out past row 1. It covers most of the holes beside its pins, so each pin on one side keeps a single free hole in column a, and the pins on the other side get none. Every part after this goes in the free rows to the right of it.

You need: 1 full-size breadboard (830 holes, 60+ rows)3 jumper wires: 3 male–male
⚠️ Leave hole a21 (the row of the ESP32's 5V pin) empty.

New wires are bright and numbered; earlier ones are faded. Hover a wire in the list to find it in the picture.

  1. Unplug the USB cable.
  2. The pictures show the board turned so row 1 is on the left, with column j at the top. If yours stands upright with row 1 at the top, column a is on the left.
  3. Turn the ESP32 so its antenna points toward row 1 and hangs over the end of the board. Its row of pins starting with 3V3 goes into column b; the row starting with GND, TX, RX goes into column j. The first pins go in row 1, so the last ones are in row 22. Press down evenly on both rows of pins, not on the metal can.
  4. Each wire to an ESP32 pin goes into column a in the same row as that pin: the only hole beside it that the ESP32 doesn't cover.

Connect

✅ Test it: Plug the USB cable back in: the clock starts as before. With a multimeter, the top + and − rails read about 3.3 V. Before you measure, check the meter's red lead is in the socket marked V, not A or mA, and the dial is on DC volts: on amps the meter shorts the supply and the ESP32 restarts.
Not reading 3.3 V on the rails? Check in this order
  1. Set the meter up. Red lead in the V socket, not A or mA: this is the most common mistake, and on amps the meter shorts the supply (the ESP32's light flashes as it restarts). Turn the dial to DC volts (V with a straight line; the 20 V range if it isn't auto-ranging). Black lead in COM. Meter probes are often too thick to reach the metal inside a breadboard hole: push the male end of a spare jumper into the hole and touch the probe to that instead.
  2. Is the ESP32 on? With the USB cable in the port marked USB, the board's small power LED should be lit and the clock's page should open. If not, try another cable and USB port before anything else.
  3. Measure on the ESP32 itself. Red probe on the solder joint of the 3V3 pin, black on the joint of a G pin. It should read about 3.3 V. If it reads 0 V, the board isn't getting power (cable or port). If it reads well under 3 V, or the board gets warm, unplug at once and look for solder bridging two header pins.
  4. Measure the 3V3 pin's row. Keep black on the G joint and put red in hole a1. 3.3 V here means the pin is making contact. 0 V means it isn't: press the ESP32 down firmly (the pins should disappear into the holes), and count the rows to check the 3V3 pin is really in the row you think.
  5. Measure the + rail. Keep black on the G joint and put red in the top + rail, near where the orange wire goes in. 0 V here: the orange wire isn't in the rail (check it is in the rail row by the red line, marked +, not the blue − row), or the jumper is broken: swap it for another.
  6. Check the rail runs the whole length. Many full-size breadboards split each rail in the middle; look for a break in the red and blue lines halfway along. Put red in the + rail at the far end. If it reads 0 V there but 3.3 V near the wire, the rail is split: bridge the two halves with a short jumper, on the − rails too.
  7. Measure + rail to − rail. Now red in the top + rail, black in the top − rail. If the earlier checks passed but this reads 0 V, the − rail isn't connected to ground: check the black wire from hole a22 to the bottom − rail, and the black wire joining the top and bottom − rails at row 60.
  8. Reads −3.3 V. The probes are swapped. Nothing is wrong.
  9. The ESP32's light flashes when you touch the probes on. Stop: the meter is shorting the supply and the board restarts each time. Usually the dial is on current (A or mA) or the red lead is in the A or mA socket: move it to V and the dial to DC volts. On amps the meter can blow its internal fuse, so check it on a battery afterwards. Otherwise a probe tip is touching two pins at once, or the black probe is touching the RST pin (it sits next to the 3V3 pins): probe the breadboard holes rather than the pins.
  10. No meter? Skip ahead to the buttons and the front display: if they work, the rails are fine.
Not working?
The ESP32 doesn't start on the breadboard
A pin may be folded under the board. Lift it out gently, straighten the pin and press it in again.
The ESP32 goes dark when you add the wires
The orange wire is in a ground row or rail. It must start in a1 (the row of the first pin, 3V3) and end in the top + rail.

Light sensor

⏱ 5 min

This step uses two separate parts: the light sensor and a 10 kΩ resistor. The sensor alone does nothing: the resistor sits under it, between the sensor and ground, and the ESP32 reads the voltage where the two meet. That voltage rises as the room gets brighter. Neither part has a right way round.

You need: GL5528 light sensor (round disc)10 kΩ resistor (a separate part: striped cylinder)2 jumper wires: 2 male–male
⚠️ Two parts, not one. If you only put the round sensor in, the reading sits near 4095 whatever the light. And check the resistor is 10 kΩ (ten thousand ohms), not 10 Ω: they come in the same kind of bag, and 10 Ω reads near 0 all the time.

New wires are bright and numbered; earlier ones are faded. Hover a wire in the list to find it in the picture.

The two parts

Place the parts

  1. Light sensor (the round disc with a squiggly line on it): legs in h45 and h48. Either way round.
  2. 10 kΩ resistor (bands brown-black-orange, or brown-black-black-red on 5-band resistors; the BOJACK bag says 10KΩ): one leg in j48, the same row as the sensor's second leg; the other leg in the top − rail (the row by the blue line), about row 49. Either way round.

Connect

✅ Test it: In the night settings, watch sensor now next to "Dark below". It goes up with a torch on the sensor and down when you cover it with a finger.
Not working?
Always about 0
The sensor leg isn't in row 45 or the orange wire isn't on the + rail.
Always about 4000 or more, even in a dim room
The ESP32 is seeing the full 3.3 V. Either the 10 kΩ resistor is missing or isn't reaching the − rail (one leg in the same row as the sensor's second leg, row 48; the other in the − rail by the blue line), or the pink wire is in the sensor's first row (45, the 3.3 V side) instead of row 48.
7

⏱ 0 min

The clock module connects to ESP32 pins 1 and 2. On one breadboard those pins are in column j, and the ESP32 covers every hole beside them, so there is nowhere to plug its wires. Skip this step: the clock runs fine without the module, setting its time from the internet, and the page shows no RTC.

You need: Nothing for now
  1. Test the module when the electronics move to the perfboard (assembly step 4), or switch to the two-breadboard layout at the top of this page.
✅ Test it: Nothing to test yet. The clock's page says no RTC, which is expected.
Not working?
I want to test it now
Use the Plugged in across two breadboards layout at the top of the page: there, pins 1 and 2 have free holes.

Connect

Not working?
Reads 0 V

1

Flash the firmware

⏱ 10 min

No wiring yet. Get the ESP32 running first, on its own, so you know the board and the firmware are good before anything else is connected.

You need: ESP32-S3 boardUSB-C data cableComputer
  1. Plug the USB-C cable into the port marked USB on the ESP32 (the board has two; this one carries the log).
  2. Flash the firmware from the Firmware page: the web flasher needs nothing installed.
  3. Open a serial monitor at 115200 baud (the web flasher has one, or PlatformIO's monitor).
  4. On your phone, join the Wi-Fi network CeilingClock-Setup and pick your home network.
✅ Test it: Open http://ceilingclock.local/ on your phone or computer. You should see the clock's page with the time and a green synced just now.
Not working?
ceilingclock.local doesn't open
Some Android phones don't support .local names. Use the IP address printed in the serial monitor instead.
Nothing in the serial monitor
Use the port marked USB, not UART, at 115200 baud. Some USB-C cables only carry power: try another.
No CeilingClock-Setup network
Press the RST button on the ESP32 and wait 20 seconds.
2

Power rails

⏱ 5 min

The two rails along the top of the breadboard become 3.3 V (from the ESP32) and ground. Every small module will plug into them. A wire over the right-hand end joins the top ground rail to the bottom one.

You need: Breadboard3 jumper wires: 2 female–male, 1 male–male

New wires are bright and numbered; earlier ones are faded. Hover a wire in the list to find it in the picture.

Connect

✅ Test it: Nothing to see yet. If you have a multimeter, the top + and − rails should read about 3.3 V with the USB cable plugged in. Before you measure, check the meter's red lead is in the socket marked V, not A or mA, and the dial is on DC volts: on amps the meter shorts the supply and the ESP32 restarts.
Not reading 3.3 V on the rails? Check in this order
  1. Set the meter up. Red lead in the V socket, not A or mA: this is the most common mistake, and on amps the meter shorts the supply (the ESP32's light flashes as it restarts). Turn the dial to DC volts (V with a straight line; the 20 V range if it isn't auto-ranging). Black lead in COM. Meter probes are often too thick to reach the metal inside a breadboard hole: push the male end of a spare jumper into the hole and touch the probe to that instead.
  2. Is the ESP32 on? With the USB cable in the port marked USB, the board's small power LED should be lit and the clock's page should open. If not, try another cable and USB port before anything else.
  3. Measure on the ESP32 itself. Red probe on the solder joint of the 3V3 pin, black on the joint of a G pin. It should read about 3.3 V. If it reads 0 V, the board isn't getting power (cable or port). If it reads well under 3 V, or the board gets warm, unplug at once and look for solder bridging two header pins.
  4. Measure the 3V3 pin's row. Keep black on the G joint and touch red to the male end of the orange wire. 0 V means the female end isn't gripping the pin: push it fully on, or try another jumper.
  5. Measure the + rail. Keep black on the G joint and put red in the top + rail, near where the orange wire goes in. 0 V here: the orange wire isn't in the rail (check it is in the rail row by the red line, marked +, not the blue − row), or the jumper is broken: swap it for another.
  6. Check the rail runs the whole length. Many full-size breadboards split each rail in the middle; look for a break in the red and blue lines halfway along. Put red in the + rail at the far end. If it reads 0 V there but 3.3 V near the wire, the rail is split: bridge the two halves with a short jumper, on the − rails too.
  7. Measure + rail to − rail. Now red in the top + rail, black in the top − rail. If the earlier checks passed but this reads 0 V, the − rail isn't connected to ground: check the black wire from the ESP32's G pin (by the USB ports) to the top − rail, and the black wire joining the two − rails at the right-hand end.
  8. Reads −3.3 V. The probes are swapped. Nothing is wrong.
  9. The ESP32's light flashes when you touch the probes on. Stop: the meter is shorting the supply and the board restarts each time. Usually the dial is on current (A or mA) or the red lead is in the A or mA socket: move it to V and the dial to DC volts. On amps the meter can blow its internal fuse, so check it on a battery afterwards. Otherwise a probe tip is touching two pins at once, or the black probe is touching the RST pin (it sits next to the 3V3 pins): probe the breadboard holes rather than the pins.
  10. No meter? Skip ahead to the buttons and the front display: if they work, the rails are fine.
Not working?
The ESP32 goes dark or resets when you plug in the wire
The 3V3 wire is in the − rail or touching G. Unplug USB and check: orange to +, black to −.
3

Buttons

⏱ 10 min

For testing, use two small 4-legged push buttons; the 16 mm panel buttons go in later. Each one sits across the gap in the middle of the breadboard. Wire to diagonally opposite legs: that way it works whichever way round the button sits.

You need: 2 small 6 × 6 mm push buttons (from your tactile switch kit)4 jumper wires: 2 female–male, 2 male–male

New wires are bright and numbered; earlier ones are faded. Hover a wire in the list to find it in the picture.

Place the parts

  1. Push button A across the gap in the middle: two legs in row 3, two in row 5, one each side of the gap.
  2. Push button B across the gap in the middle: two legs in row 8, two in row 10, one each side of the gap.

Connect

✅ Test it: On the clock's page, press button B: the Front display button on the page flips between on and off. Now press B and keep holding it: 3 seconds after you pressed, Projector flips on the page (the page can take another second to show it). Let go after it flips; letting go sooner counts as a short press. (Button A snoozes an alarm; you'll try it later.)
Not working?
Nothing happens
Check the wires go to diagonally opposite legs (j3 and a5, j8 and a10) and that the button straddles the gap.
It acts as if always pressed
The button is turned so both wires land on legs that are always connected. Turn it 90°.

✅ Test it: The display shows the time within a second. On the settings page, change the front display's brightness: it follows.
Not working?
Display stays blank
CLK and DIO swapped? VCC must go to the + rail (3.3 V).
Shows 88:88 or garbage
A loose jumper: push each one firmly onto its pin.

Not working?
Blank or solid black

No backlight

6

Light sensor

⏱ 5 min

This step uses two separate parts: the light sensor and a 10 kΩ resistor. The sensor alone does nothing: the resistor sits under it, between the sensor and ground, and the ESP32 reads the voltage where the two meet. That voltage rises as the room gets brighter. Neither part has a right way round.

You need: GL5528 light sensor (round disc)10 kΩ resistor (a separate part: striped cylinder)2 jumper wires: 1 female–male, 1 male–male
⚠️ Two parts, not one. If you only put the round sensor in, the reading sits near 4095 whatever the light. And check the resistor is 10 kΩ (ten thousand ohms), not 10 Ω: they come in the same kind of bag, and 10 Ω reads near 0 all the time.

New wires are bright and numbered; earlier ones are faded. Hover a wire in the list to find it in the picture.

The two parts

Place the parts

  1. Light sensor (the round disc with a squiggly line on it): legs in h13 and h16. Either way round.
  2. 10 kΩ resistor (bands brown-black-orange, or brown-black-black-red on 5-band resistors; the BOJACK bag says 10KΩ): one leg in j16, the same row as the sensor's second leg; the other leg in the top − rail (the row by the blue line), about row 17. Either way round.

Connect

✅ Test it: In the night settings, watch sensor now next to "Dark below". It goes up with a torch on the sensor and down when you cover it with a finger.
Not working?
Always about 0
The sensor leg isn't in row 13 or the orange wire isn't on the + rail.
Always about 4000 or more, even in a dim room
The ESP32 is seeing the full 3.3 V. Either the 10 kΩ resistor is missing or isn't reaching the − rail (one leg in the same row as the sensor's second leg, row 16; the other in the − rail by the blue line), or the pink wire is in the sensor's first row (13, the 3.3 V side) instead of row 16.

★

Bonus: see it on the ceiling

⏱ 15 min

Once the LCD has its window cut (assembly step 5), you can try the projector by hand in a dark room before printing anything.

  1. Point the LED up, sitting on its metal.
  2. Hold a piece of baking paper about 10 mm above it, and the LCD, glass up, about 30 mm above it.
  3. Hold the lens about 106 mm above the LCD, look at the ceiling, and move the lens up and down until the digits are sharp. That's what the focus ring does in the finished clock.
  4. Use Mirror left/right and Flip projection on the clock's page until it reads right from where you lie. In the clock the mirror adds one more flip, so expect to change Mirror left/right once it's built.

Done?

When every step passes, move the same connections onto the perfboard (assembly step 4). Two things change in the finished clock: the 16 mm buttons replace the small ones, and the 5 V supply also feeds the ESP32's 5V pin, so from then on leave the computer unplugged and update the firmware over Wi-Fi. The full pin list is on the wiring page.
